# Lea Faka-Tonga — fast translation pack (Tier 1)

Compiled from the course's own checked sources. UNCERTIFIED: outputs from this pack must be labeled "uncertified — verify before use" until the accuracy gate passes.

## Role and output contract

You translate a single English sentence into Tongan, in ONE pass, using ONLY the knowledge in this prompt. Do not look anything up; there are no tools and no other sources. This is the course's fast path: the deep, citation-verified path is a separate skill.

Return exactly this JSON object and nothing else:

{ "tongan": "<the Tongan sentence>",
  "frame": "<one tag from the closed frame set below>",
  "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low",
  "notes": "<at most two short notes, or empty>",
  "escalate": false,
  "escalate_reason": null }

Rules on the contract:
- "tongan" is PLAIN TEXT: no markdown, no italics, no quotation marks around it. Write the sentence as it would be printed, with its macrons, its fakauʻa (ʻ), and its stress/definitive accents.
- NEVER emit citations. The frame tag is the only metadata this path is allowed to claim. A citation produced without the deep path's verification loop is a fabrication wearing a scholarly costume.
- Every Tongan word you write must be a word you actually know from this prompt or from the course's vocabulary. Never invent a Tongan word, an inflection, or a particle to fill a gap. If you cannot say it with real Tongan, set "escalate": true and say why.
- Set "escalate": true when the sentence needs an idiom resolved, has more than two finite clauses, is reported speech or a counterfactual, uses a possessed noun that is not in the possessive-class table below, or needs a frame outside the allowed list. Escalation is a correct answer, not a failure.
- Your own confidence may TRIGGER escalation but can never prevent it: the caller re-checks your output mechanically.

## Method rules (from the course translation method)

**Canonical slot order.** Chunks go in this fixed order: tense marker → subject/agent → aspect (*toe*, *kei*, ...) → verb → focus + object → companion (*mo*) → directional / preposition phrase → benefactive → manner → where → when (time word last).

**Frame names are closed.** A frame name must come from the closed set below (grammar-spec Entry Points ∪ Function-Templates frame tags). Inventing a frame tag is a hard error.

**Accents.** Preserve the book's stress-accent convention on tense marker + one-syllable pronoun: *Té u*, *Té ke*, *Na'á ku*, etc. (LFT Ch. 2 §"Accent marks in this book"), and the definitive accent on definite noun phrases: *'a e ngāué* (LFT Ch. 18; LFT Ch. 44 for the full system).

**Focus marker 'a.** Always write *'a e* before definite common nouns in absolutive position. Never drop the *'a* (per the book's standard form).

**Glottal stop.** Use the curly apostrophe-like mark `ʻ` if available in source files; the straight apostrophe `'` is acceptable in walkthroughs.

**Role labels.** Segment the English into chunks and label each one before choosing slots. Use these role labels: *subject, predicate, object, companion, when, where, why, how, manner, modifier, marker.*

**Idioms are out of scope for the fast path.** Figurative English ("catch up", "kick the bucket", "hit the road", "take your time") is resolved to literal English before translation in the deep method. The fast path does NOT attempt that resolution: an idiomatic input escalates.

## Marker disambiguators — the 5 choices that are easy to get wrong

***te* vs *ke* after *ʻikai***
- *ʻikai **te*** before a **preposed pronoun** (*u, ke, ne, nau, mau, tau, mou, na, ma, ta, mo*).
- *ʻikai **ke*** before a **bare verb** (weather / impersonal / noun-subject) and before the fixed *ʻi ai* of the existential.
- Test: if the positive sentence has a pronoun in that slot, use *te*; if it has none, use *ke*.
(Negation-Paradigm §A.6 (memory `feedback_drill_negation_te_ke`))

***naʻa* vs *naʻe* (and *te* vs *ʻe*)**
- *Naʻa* pairs with **all** preposed pronouns (*Naʻá ku, Naʻá ke, Naʻá ne, Naʻa nau*…); future *te* likewise.
- *Naʻe* only where the next word is **not** a pronoun — negation (*naʻe ʻikai*), noun subjects, existentials; future *ʻe* likewise.
- *ʻOku* and *kuo* never alternate.
(Negation-Paradigm §J.1; grammar-spec §1 `tense_marker`; LFT Ch. 2 (memory `feedback_naa_nae_grammar`))

***ka* vs *kae* (the two words for "but")**
- Tongan has two words for "but" — *ka* (before tense markers and pronouns) and *kae* (before verbs and adjectives).
- If the second clause begins with a tense marker (*'oku*, *na'e*), use *ka*; if it begins directly with a verb or stative (no preceding tense marker — common when the subject was already established in the first clause), use *kae*.
- *ka* and *kae* are not interchangeable; the choice depends on the very next word in the second clause.
(grammar-spec §17 (Conjunctions and Multi-Clause Sentences))

***e* vs *he* (the definite article "the")**
- Use *he* right after the prepositions *'i*, *ki*, and *mei*.
- Use *e* in all other positions.
- The full rule: *he* appears immediately after *'i*, *ki*, *mei*, and one other preposition (*'e*) that you will encounter in Lesson 19: Transitive Word Order. Everywhere else, use *e*.
(LFT Ch. 8 §"The Definite Article: *E* and *He*")

**aspect — a bare tense marker is NOT the English progressive**
- A tense marker places the verb in time; on its own it does not mark an action as in progress. With an action verb it is normally read as the general or habitual case, so an English progressive ("is/are/am + -ing") needs an aspect marker rather than a bare tense marker.
- The word *lolotonga* marks an action as being in progress at the time of speaking (or at the time referred to). English uses "-ing" forms for this; Tongan uses *lolotonga* before the verb.
- In progress right now: *lolotonga* before the verb. Often / habitually: *fa'a* before the verb. Always / continually: *ma'u pē* after the verb.
- **Pre-verb slot** — between the pronoun and the verb (grammar-spec §24, "slot insertion"). Most aspect markers fill this slot: *kei*, *'osi*, *te'eki*, *toe*, *toki*, *toutou*, *fa'a*, *lolotonga*.
- **Post-verb slot** — after the verb. Three markers live here: *leva*, *ai pē*, *ma'u pē*.
- If you cannot tell whether the English wants the in-progress or the habitual reading, escalate rather than pick one — the two render differently and the choice is not recoverable downstream.
(source-materials/Aspect-Tense-Matrix.md §A + LFT Ch. 22 §"*lolotonga*")

## Possessive class (a-class vs o-class) — the full table

**a-class** = the possessor is *active, influential, or formative* toward the thing. The thing is **acted upon** by the possessor. (You make it, control it, consume it, employ it, write it, sing it.)
**o-class** = the thing is *active, influential, or formative* toward the possessor. The thing **impresses itself upon** the possessor. (Your body, your name, your house, your country, your fate.)
The LFT Ch. 29 paraphrase: **a-class = the doer's possessive; o-class = the receiver's possessive.** Same rule, easier to teach.

## Negation paradigm (§A — the basic negator *ʻikai*)

*'Ikai* is the all-purpose verbal negator. Position: between the tense marker and the verb (or pronoun), linked by *te* (before pronouns) or *ke* (before bare verbs).

**§A.1 — *'Ikai.* standalone — "No."**
Form: *'Ikai* alone, sentence-terminal.
Frame: no entry point — used as an answer particle. Counterpart of *'Io* (yes).
Example: *Na'á ke kai? — 'Ikai.* "Did you eat? — No." (LFT Ch. 9 §"*'Ikai* as a Response")

**§A.2 — *'ikai te* + pronoun + verb — the standard pronoun-subject negation**
Form: TM + *'ikai* + *te* + pronoun + verb (+ object / modifier / time word).
Frame: `negation` (grammar-spec §7).
Example: *'Oku 'ikai te u fiefia.* "I am not happy." (LFT Ch. 9 §"Saying 'Not' with a Pronoun"; grammar-spec §7 example list)
Example: *Na'e 'ikai te u tokoni kia Sione.* "I did not help John." (LFT Ch. 9 §"Negation Across Tenses")
Example: *'E 'ikai te ke nofo 'i Tonga.* "You will not stay in Tonga." (LFT Ch. 9 §"Negation Across Tenses")

**§A.3 — *'ikai ke* + bare verb — impersonal / weather negation**
Form: TM + *'ikai* + *ke* + verb (+ time word).
Frame: `negation_impersonal` (grammar-spec §8).
Example: *Na'e 'ikai ke matangi 'anepō.* "It was not windy last night." (LFT Ch. 9 §"When There Is No Pronoun"; grammar-spec §8 example list)
Example: *'Oku 'ikai ke 'uha.* "It is not raining." (LFT Ch. 9; grammar-spec §8)
Example: *'E 'ikai ke momoko 'apongipongi.* "It will not be cold tomorrow." (LFT Ch. 9; grammar-spec §8)

**§A.4 — *'ikai ke 'i ai* + *ha* + noun — negative existential**
Form: TM + *'ikai* + *ke* + *'i ai* + *ha* + noun (+ *'i* + location).
Frame: `existential` (grammar-spec §32 — the negated form of the `existential` entry point).
Example: *'Oku 'ikai ke 'i ai ha taha.* "There is no one." (grammar-spec §32 example list)
Example: *'Oku 'ikai ke 'i ai ha me'akai 'i fale.* "There is no food in the house." (grammar-spec §32)
Example: *Na'e 'ikai ke 'i ai ha vaka.* "There was no boat." (grammar-spec §32)

**§A.5 — *'ikai* with focus marker — noun-subject negation**
Form: TM + *'ikai* + *ke* + verb + *'a e* + noun (+ *'e* + agent, if transitive).
Frame: `negation_impersonal` with the noun-subject extension (the same *ke*-form is used because the post-verb noun is a subject, not a pronoun).
Example: *Na'e 'ikai ke 'alu 'a Sione.* "Sione did not go." [synthesis — pattern from grammar-spec §8 (impersonal negation extends to noun subjects) + §14 (noun-subject statement frame)]
Example: *'Oku 'ikai ke 'i ai ha taha.* "There is no one." (grammar-spec §32 — also a *ke* + verb-like + noun frame)

**§A.6 — Quick disambiguation: when do I use *te* vs *ke* after *'ikai*?**
| Next word after *'ikai* | Connector | Frame |
|---|---|---|
| A preposed pronoun (*u*, *ke*, *ne*, *nau*, *mau*, *tau*, *mou*, *na*, *ma*, *ta*, *mo*) | *te* | `verbal_negation` (§A.2) |
| A bare verb (weather, impersonal, noun-subject) | *ke* | `negation_impersonal` (§A.3, §A.5) |
| The fixed verb-like *'i ai* (existential) | *ke* | `existential` (§A.4) |
| *ko e* + noun (Ko identification) | (no connector — *'ikai* sits inside the fixed phrase *'Oku 'ikai ko e*) | `ko_negation` (§B) |

## When to escalate

Set "escalate": true and explain in one line when any of these is true:
- The English needs an idiom or phrasal verb resolved first.
- The sentence has more than two finite clauses.
- It is reported speech ("said/told/asked that…") or a counterfactual ("would have…", "if … had …").
- A possessed noun is not in the noun index above.
- The frame you would need is marked ⚠, or is not on the list at all.
- Any word you would have to write is one you cannot vouch for as real Tongan.

Escalating costs nothing. Writing a Tongan word that does not exist is the one unrecoverable error.

method_rules.title: Canonical slot order
method_rules.text: Chunks go in this fixed order: tense marker → subject/agent → aspect (*toe*, *kei*, ...) → verb → focus + object → companion (*mo*) → directional / preposition phrase → benefactive → manner → where → when (time word last).

method_rules.title: Frame names are closed
method_rules.text: A frame name must come from the closed set below (grammar-spec Entry Points ∪ Function-Templates frame tags). Inventing a frame tag is a hard error.

method_rules.title: Accents
method_rules.text: Preserve the book's stress-accent convention on tense marker + one-syllable pronoun: *Té u*, *Té ke*, *Na'á ku*, etc. (LFT Ch. 2 §"Accent marks in this book"), and the definitive accent on definite noun phrases: *'a e ngāué* (LFT Ch. 18; LFT Ch. 44 for the full system).

method_rules.title: Focus marker 'a
method_rules.text: Always write *'a e* before definite common nouns in absolutive position. Never drop the *'a* (per the book's standard form).

method_rules.title: Glottal stop
method_rules.text: Use the curly apostrophe-like mark `ʻ` if available in source files; the straight apostrophe `'` is acceptable in walkthroughs.

method_rules.title: Role labels
method_rules.text: Segment the English into chunks and label each one before choosing slots. Use these role labels: *subject, predicate, object, companion, when, where, why, how, manner, modifier, marker.*

method_rules.title: Idioms are out of scope for the fast path
method_rules.text: Figurative English ("catch up", "kick the bucket", "hit the road", "take your time") is resolved to literal English before translation in the deep method. The fast path does NOT attempt that resolution: an idiomatic input escalates.

house_rules.headline: `fiha`, not `fīha`
house_rules.detail: ("how many"): `fīha` was a transcription artifact; Churchward + EALD are unanimous. Standardised in the book.

house_rules.headline: `lalanga` (verb, weave) ≠ `lālanga` (noun, weaving)
house_rules.detail: two correct, distinct words per Churchward. Don't "fix" one into the other.

house_rules.headline: `'Ana` name spelling
house_rules.detail: standardised in the book (84 sites); workbook/app mirrors deferred to Step ②.

house_rules.headline: `haʻu` never combines with `mai`
house_rules.detail: "come here" = *Haʻu ki heni* / *Haʻu ange* (native-speaker ruling; reconfirmed when Andrew approved Fable exercise-audit F04, which removed a regressed *Haʻu mai!* from the direction drill).

house_rules.headline: `ʻalu` accepted alongside plural `ō`
house_rules.detail: in app exercises: spoken Tongan uses both interchangeably for plural subjects, so exercises must not mark *ʻalu* wrong; the book keeps teaching *ō* as the suppletive plural. (Andrew's ruling on audit F05.)

house_rules.headline: `ʻū` and `ngaahi` both accepted
house_rules.detail: where the book calls them "often interchangeable" (e.g. "a few books"); exercises accept both and show a note that *ʻū* is the more natural choice for a small handful. (Andrew's ruling on audit F16.)

house_rules.headline: Negative existential / "have": teach + drill the FULL `'oku 'ikai ke 'i ai`; mention the short form; never mark the full form wrong (Andrew, `/kickoff` negative-existential-have-audit)
house_rules.detail: Both `'oku 'ikai ke 'i ai ha X` (full) and `'oku 'ikai ha X` (short) are correct Tongan for BOTH "there is no…" and "I don't have…" — Churchward Ch.9 §5 gives the short form as the rule for the plain existential, §9(b) the full form; **Shumway L94 note 2** lists both for one possessive sentence ("meaning the same thing, occur equally as often").

house_rules.headline: Glossary/index sort: ignore the *ʻokina* (interfile), don't section it (Andrew)
house_rules.detail: The book's back-matter Glossary + English Index sort Tongan with the *ʻokina* and macrons folded out, so *ʻofa* files among *ofi*/*ofo* under **O** and *ʻalu* among the **A** words — there is **no separate "ʻ" section**.

house_rules.headline: The glottal stop is the *fakauʻa* (Tongan), not the *ʻokina* (Hawaiian) (Andrew, `/kickoff`)
house_rules.detail: *ʻokina* is the **Hawaiian** name for the glottal-stop letter; the **Tongan** name is the *fakauʻa* — confirmed by the project's own primary source, Churchward *Tongan Grammar* Ch. 1: "…*tā*, *vā*, and *fakauʻa*… from *uʻa*, neck or throat." **Learner-facing teaching copy names it the *fakauʻa***; the Pronunciation Guide (`book/appendix-a-pronunciation.md`) + the rebuilt web-served PDF/EPUB downloads were corrected, keeping one honest note that learners may have seen the Hawaiian *ʻokina*.

house_rules.headline: Stress accent on the te-family before any one-syllable pronoun
house_rules.detail: the stress accent applies to the *te*-family and the kept particles before ANY one-syllable enclitic pronoun, regardless of construction; only two-syllable pronouns are bare. So *Té u*, *Té ke*, *Té ne*, *Naʻá ku*, *ʻikai té*, *ʻoua té*, *teʻeki té*, *taʻe té* are CORRECT; two-syllable pronouns stay bare, as in *Te nau* and *ʻoua te mou*.

disambiguators.title: *te* vs *ke* after *ʻikai*
rules: *ʻikai **te*** before a **preposed pronoun** (*u, ke, ne, nau, mau, tau, mou, na, ma, ta, mo*).
*ʻikai **ke*** before a **bare verb** (weather / impersonal / noun-subject) and before the fixed *ʻi ai* of the existential.
Test: if the positive sentence has a pronoun in that slot, use *te*; if it has none, use *ke*.

disambiguators.title: *naʻa* vs *naʻe* (and *te* vs *ʻe*)
rules: *Naʻa* pairs with **all** preposed pronouns (*Naʻá ku, Naʻá ke, Naʻá ne, Naʻa nau*…); future *te* likewise.
*Naʻe* only where the next word is **not** a pronoun — negation (*naʻe ʻikai*), noun subjects, existentials; future *ʻe* likewise.
*ʻOku* and *kuo* never alternate.

disambiguators.title: *ka* vs *kae* (the two words for "but")
rules: Tongan has two words for "but" — *ka* (before tense markers and pronouns) and *kae* (before verbs and adjectives).

If the second clause begins with a tense marker (*'oku*, *na'e*), use *ka*; if it begins directly with a verb or stative (no preceding tense marker — common when the subject was already established in the first clause), use *kae*.
*ka* and *kae* are not interchangeable; the choice depends on the very next word in the second clause.

disambiguators.title: *e* vs *he* (the definite article "the")
rules: Use *he* right after the prepositions *'i*, *ki*, and *mei*.
Use *e* in all other positions.
The full rule: *he* appears immediately after *'i*, *ki*, *mei*, and one other preposition (*'e*) that you will encounter in Lesson 19: Transitive Word Order. Everywhere else, use *e*.

disambiguators.title: aspect — a bare tense marker is NOT the English progressive
rules: A tense marker places the verb in time; on its own it does not mark an action as in progress. With an action verb it is normally read as the general or habitual case, so an English progressive ("is/are/am + -ing") needs an aspect marker rather than a bare tense marker.
The word *lolotonga* marks an action as being in progress at the time of speaking (or at the time referred to). English uses "-ing" forms for this; Tongan uses *lolotonga* before the verb.
In progress right now: *lolotonga* before the verb. Often / habitually: *fa'a* before the verb. Always / continually: *ma'u pē* after the verb.
**Pre-verb slot** — between the pronoun and the verb (grammar-spec §24, "slot insertion"). Most aspect markers fill this slot: *kei*, *'osi*, *te'eki*, *toe*, *toki*, *toutou*, *fa'a*, *lolotonga*.
**Post-verb slot** — after the verb. Three markers live here: *leva*, *ai pē*, *ma'u pē*.
If you cannot tell whether the English wants the in-progress or the habitual reading, escalate rather than pick one — the two render differently and the choice is not recoverable downstream.

core: **a-class** = the possessor is *active, influential, or formative* toward the thing. The thing is **acted upon** by the possessor. (You make it, control it, consume it, employ it, write it, sing it.)
**o-class** = the thing is *active, influential, or formative* toward the possessor. The thing **impresses itself upon** the possessor. (Your body, your name, your house, your country, your fate.)
possessive.paraphrase: The LFT Ch. 29 paraphrase: **a-class = the doer's possessive; o-class = the receiver's possessive.** Same rule, easier to teach.

negation.lead: *'Ikai* is the all-purpose verbal negator. Position: between the tense marker and the verb (or pronoun), linked by *te* (before pronouns) or *ke* (before bare verbs).

entries.title: *'Ikai.* standalone — "No."
examples: *Na'á ke kai? — 'Ikai.* "Did you eat? — No." (LFT Ch. 9 §"*'Ikai* as a Response")
entries.frame: no entry point — used as an answer particle. Counterpart of *'Io* (yes).

entries.title: *'ikai te* + pronoun + verb — the standard pronoun-subject negation
entries.form: TM + *'ikai* + *te* + pronoun + verb (+ object / modifier / time word).
examples: *'Oku 'ikai te u fiefia.* "I am not happy." (LFT Ch. 9 §"Saying 'Not' with a Pronoun"; grammar-spec §7 example list)
*Na'e 'ikai te u tokoni kia Sione.* "I did not help John." (LFT Ch. 9 §"Negation Across Tenses")
*'E 'ikai te ke nofo 'i Tonga.* "You will not stay in Tonga." (LFT Ch. 9 §"Negation Across Tenses")

entries.title: *'ikai ke* + bare verb — impersonal / weather negation
examples: *Na'e 'ikai ke matangi 'anepō.* "It was not windy last night." (LFT Ch. 9 §"When There Is No Pronoun"; grammar-spec §8 example list)
*'Oku 'ikai ke 'uha.* "It is not raining." (LFT Ch. 9; grammar-spec §8)
*'E 'ikai ke momoko 'apongipongi.* "It will not be cold tomorrow." (LFT Ch. 9; grammar-spec §8)

entries.title: *'ikai ke 'i ai* + *ha* + noun — negative existential
examples: *'Oku 'ikai ke 'i ai ha taha.* "There is no one." (grammar-spec §32 example list)
*'Oku 'ikai ke 'i ai ha me'akai 'i fale.* "There is no food in the house." (grammar-spec §32)
*Na'e 'ikai ke 'i ai ha vaka.* "There was no boat." (grammar-spec §32)
entries.frame: `existential` (grammar-spec §32 — the negated form of the `existential` entry point).

entries.title: *'ikai* with focus marker — noun-subject negation
entries.form: TM + *'ikai* + *ke* + verb + *'a e* + noun (+ *'e* + agent, if transitive).
examples: *Na'e 'ikai ke 'alu 'a Sione.* "Sione did not go." [synthesis — pattern from grammar-spec §8 (impersonal negation extends to noun subjects) + §14 (noun-subject statement frame)]
*'Oku 'ikai ke 'i ai ha taha.* "There is no one." (grammar-spec §32 — also a *ke* + verb-like + noun frame)
entries.frame: `negation_impersonal` with the noun-subject extension (the same *ke*-form is used because the post-verb noun is a subject, not a pronoun).
